items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It was great to play with Gary and Benny... Keith and I were asked by Gary Peacock to come do his record for ECM... Manfred thought it might be a good idea if maybe we formed a trio... The Out-Of-Towners with Keith Jarrett and Gary Peacock, essentially The Standards Trio

ctx.x: …Just wanted to return for the chronology about the second recording date that is crediting you as a leader called, Have You Heard? recorded in Tokyo. Is that accurate?

Yes, it was. How that came about was the Japanese promoter Koinuma (?) used to have what they called… It was one of those “drum” things which featured me, Mel Lewis, Roy Haynes and his Hip Ensemble, and a Japanese drummer named George Ozutka (?), who kind of played a little like Roy, but was a really nice drummer. While I was there, Benny Maupin was also in Roy’s Hip Ensemble, and Bill Wood on bass in Roy’s band. So, what would happen is we were doing this tour and each of us would do a drum solo or we would take…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: I had my old bands, other good musicians, Keith Jarrett and Gary Peacock’s Standards Trio.

ctx.x: How about, this is not a person but a record label, ECM? Did you feel that you needed to adjust your style when you played for that —

Not really, because actually it was actually freeing because Manfred Eicher, the producer there, wanted to bring out the best situation, an artistic situation, in music. And it was actually my cymbal work got amplified on a lot of recordings of ECM because Manfred liked detail. And he also liked spontaneity as well as written compositions. And also ECM had a sound that people really liked, and an artistic thing with the covers and it’s still going on today. So it was more about the art of the music rather than…

and they also supported the musicians on their recordings, their touring. So yeah I mean I had a lot of fun recording for ECM. I had my old bands, other good musicians, Keith Jarrett and Gary Peacock’s Standards Trio. So yeah, there was a lot of room to experiment but at a high level of creativity.
